title: Rooming houses and home cooking in the South
summary: Bands stayed in private homes or rooming houses, ate home-cooked meals and knew hosts in many towns.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: What about accomodations in the South?
Well, we usually would stay at somebody's home. And they had -- some of the big cities had a little

colored hotels in the South, but mostly rooming houses is where we would stay. Some people would just do that, put bands up and things of this sort, you know. And we knew a lot of these places because a lot of different bands would stop there, you know. And they would cook. A lot of these people at these homes, they would cook and you'd pay so much for a meal, you know, things. So, you didn't have no problem right there, you know.

Sometimes you had problems getting to the bathroom. They didn't have that many bathrooms all the times for a big band, but it always worked out. There was always a way. We made it, you know. But you have to love music really to go through that then, you know.

But the kids never had it so good as they have it, you know. We had to -- we were more like pioneers really back there then, just blazing away, you know, making the trail. Then we got so we'd know people in different cities, and we'd probably stay with them. We'd write, you know, before we came. That happened -- if you were working and worked in a popular band, you didn't have any problem because you knew somebody almost anywhere you went. You could stay with them, you know, friends or people of this ilk, you know. You had no problems.
